clue.text: Big noise behind Private Eye

blocks.note: the magazine setting the puzzle refers to itself as 'us'

explanation.surface: Someone influential lurks behind the satirical magazine, pulling the strings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big noise' looks like a person of importance, but it is a literal din; Private Eye is where this crossword appears, so the magazine is 'us'.
explanation.definitionFit: A rumpus is a noisy commotion or uproar, so a big noise describes it well.

clue.text: Strange start to unseemly forehand tossing

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, so only that letter counts
tossing throws things about, so the letters land in a new order

explanation.surface: A tennis player begins an oddly indecent-looking forehand, with a smutty hint of 'tossing'.
explanation.walkthrough: The tennis picture hides that 'tossing' is the scrambling signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unheard-of is unprecedented and unfamiliar, so it is strange.

clue.text: Political leader's a joke, suppressing Times and Independent leaders

indicators.note: leaders are the front runners, so the first letter of each named word is used
to suppress is to hold down and enclose, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a pun is a play on words
first letters of Times and Independent

explanation.surface: A strongman stifles the press, starting with the leading newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: The Times and the Independent are British national newspapers, apt for a leader who muzzles the media.
explanation.definitionFit: Vladimir Putin is Russia's president, an example of a political leader.

clue.text: Like an earth-moving experience? One needs S and M on one in short time

indicators.note: one thing placed on another comes after it, so the final piece follows the earlier ones
pieces placed in another go inside its letters

explanation.surface: Sex so good the earth moves, though one partner needs a bit of S and M.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Did the earth move for you?' is a joke about great sex; the definition takes it literally, as an earthquake.
explanation.definitionFit: Seismic means relating to earthquakes, which literally move the earth.

clue.text: What prisoner does with Buzz's piping?

blocks.note: in British slang a prisoner 'does bird', serving time
to give someone a buzz is to give them a phone call

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about what an inmate does with Buzz's whistling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird' (from rhyming slang 'birdlime' for time) is British slang for a prison sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: Piping is the high whistling song a bird makes, which is exactly a birdcall.

clue.text: Dummy Dubya not hot about uprising attempt

indicators.note: not means without, so that letter is dropped from the name
rising up in a down clue means reading from the bottom upwards
one piece going about another wraps around it

blocks.note: Dubya is a nickname of George W. Bush
H for hot, as on taps
to have a go is to make an attempt

explanation.surface: A jibe at George W. Bush, the dummy who is cool about a rebellion attempt.
explanation.definitionFit: A dummy is a fake or imitation, so it is bogus, counterfeit.

clue.text: "Refuse Bush?" Blair snapped (Al backed out)

indicators.note: someone who backed out withdrew, so those letters leave the fodder
something snapped is broken, so the letters fall into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written: Al Gore, perhaps

explanation.surface: Tony Blair snaps at a suggestion that he refuse George Bush, while Al Gore withdraws.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' looks like a verb (pronounced re-FUSE), but it is the noun meaning waste.
explanation.definitionFit: Refuse as a noun means waste matter, which is rubbish.

clue.text: Customers etc. screwed with Nellie

indicators.note: screwed means twisted round, so the letters are turned into a new order

explanation.surface: A brothel madam's clients, and the rest, all bedded Nellie.
explanation.definitionFit: A clientele is the body of customers or clients a business serves.

clue.text: Excess of wine right for cheap flight specialist?

blocks.note: a wine lake is a surplus of unsold wine, as in the EU's

explanation.surface: Too much wine is just the thing for a budget airline expert.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Freddie Laker founded Laker Airways, whose Skytrain pioneered cheap transatlantic flights in the 1970s; the question mark flags definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Freddie Laker was a British airline entrepreneur known for low-cost fares, an example of a cheap flight specialist.

clue.text: (& 10) Very apprehensive when evacuating parts of buildings

explanation.surface: Workers grow nervous while clearing people out of sections of buildings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Evacuating' suggests clearing people from a building, but here it is the bodily sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To be 'shitting bricks' is a vulgar British idiom for being terrified or extremely nervous.

clue.text: see 9ac.
Start of interest in lavatory bowl torture

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept
one piece sits in another, so it goes inside the other's letters

blocks.note: the pan is the bowl of a toilet

explanation.surface: An interest in lavatory-bowl torture, perhaps the schoolyard practice of flushing someone's head.
explanation.definitionFit: Torture is the infliction of severe pain, and pain itself can mean torment or suffering.

clue.text: (& 26ac.) Roger conventionally adopting this view: "godless foreigners should be converted"

definitions.note: the answer is what one adopts to roger conventionally

blocks.note: first meaning: the standard sexual ..., adopted for conventional sex ('roger' is British slang for have sex with)
second meaning: the stance of a ... bent on converting heathens

explanation.surface: Someone called Roger holds the conventional opinion that unbelievers abroad need converting.
explanation.walkthrough: Roger looks like a man's name; it is British slang for having sex.
explanation.definitionFit: A position is a stance or opinion, so a missionary's view is a missionary position; it is also the common face-to-face sex position.

clue.text: Somewhat bigoted if I censor an erection?

indicators.note: somewhat means only part of the following phrase is used, a run of letters inside it

blocks.note: the letters run across bigot-ed, if, I and ce-nsor

explanation.surface: Is it narrow-minded of me to censor something rude?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the smutty reading of 'erection'; it is simply a building.
explanation.definitionFit: An erection is anything put up, a structure, and an edifice is a large building.

clue.text: French supporters — they won't go down well with typical Brits?

definitions.text: they won't go down well with typical Brits?

blocks.note: Frogs is a disparaging British nickname for the French

explanation.surface: French football fans are unpopular with the average British supporter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go down well' reads as 'be welcomed', but it is literal: swallowed.
explanation.definitionFit: Frogs' legs are a French delicacy that many British eaters find off-putting, so they will not be swallowed with relish.

clue.text: Was sick but not cast down

blocks.note: second meaning: tossed upwards rather than downwards

explanation.surface: Someone felt ill but, refusing to be dispirited, stayed cheerful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast down' reads as one phrase meaning dejected; read literally, something not cast down was cast, or thrown, the other way.
explanation.definitionFit: To throw up is an informal phrasal verb for vomiting, and literally means to toss something upwards.

clue.text: Labour less than is required!

explanation.surface: An exclamation urging the Labour party, or a lazy worker, to slacken off.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital L hints at the Labour Party, but it is simply toil; the whole clue is both wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To underwork is to do too little work, to toil less than one should.

clue.text: Member's cover-up when Tony's off round France

indicators.note: something gone off has spoiled and changed, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: R is a standard abbreviation for round
F is the international vehicle code for France

explanation.surface: A political cover-up while Tony Blair is away touring France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' suggests a Member of Parliament and 'cover-up' a scandal; Y-fronts are a classic British style of men's briefs.
explanation.definitionFit: Y-fronts are men's underpants, a garment that covers the male member.

clue.text: Extra, cheating, uses air-tube

indicators.note: what the phrase uses is drawn from within it, a run of its letters

blocks.note: the letters run across ex-tra and chea-ting

explanation.surface: A cheating diver sneaks an extra snorkel.
explanation.definitionFit: The trachea, or windpipe, is the tube carrying air to the lungs.

clue.text: "Kinky Spears draped round Democrat's leader" smears

indicators.note: kinky means twisted, so the letters of the name are bent out of order
a leader comes first, so only the opening letter is taken
something draped round another wraps it, so one set of letters goes outside the other

explanation.surface: A tabloid headline: a pop star in a compromising clinch with a politician.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged singer's surname wraps around the single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To smear something is to spread it over a surface, so smears and spreads are verb synonyms.

clue.text: Hack able to fly with Margaret since getting Bush's heart

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its centre, so only the middle letters are kept

blocks.note: Peg is a pet form of Margaret
as can mean since, giving a reason

explanation.surface: A journalist ready to flee with Margaret Thatcher after landing an interview with George Bush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hack' suggests a journalist; it is a horse, and the winged horse of Greek myth.
explanation.definitionFit: A hack is a riding horse, and Pegasus is the flying horse of Greek mythology.

clue.text: Accepting urine sample is derisory?

explanation.surface: A medical receptionist taking a specimen, wondering if it's a joke.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue's two pieces come in reverse order: 'taking a piss' becomes the adjective. 'Taking the piss' is British slang for mocking.
explanation.definitionFit: Piss-taking is British slang for mockery, so a piss-taking remark is a derisory, scornful one.

clue.text: Cyclops is cuddling girl with round figure, in a manner of speaking

indicators.note: cuddling wraps arms around someone, so the outer piece encloses the inner

blocks.note: the setter speaking of himself: I'm
Di is a short girl's name

explanation.surface: The setter, figuratively speaking, cuddles a curvaceous girl.
explanation.walkthrough: Cyclops is the setter's pseudonym, so 'Cyclops is' means 'I'm'. 'Round figure' sounds like a curvy body.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom is a characteristic expression or way of speaking particular to a language or group.

clue.text: In the way of an impotent member, head off for state, indirectly

indicators.note: with its head off a word loses its first letter

blocks.clueFragment: In the way of an impotent member
blocks.note: an impotent member hangs limp, so it behaves limply

explanation.surface: A rude description of a failed performance, delivered with innuendo.
explanation.definitionFit: To imply is to suggest something without saying it outright, stating it indirectly.

clue.text: Browse for cocaine-free dandruff?

indicators.note: free of something means without it, so that letter is taken away

blocks.note: C is slang shorthand for cocaine

explanation.surface: Shopping around for a shampoo that is free of drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cocaine-free' reads as a single adjective, but it tells you to drop the drug's letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To surf the internet is to browse it, moving idly from page to page.

clue.text: Lecher screwed stray

indicators.note: screwed means twisted, so the letters are wrenched into a new order

explanation.surface: A womaniser bedded a passing stray, crudely put.
explanation.definitionFit: A satyr is a lustful woodland god of Greek myth, and by extension a lecherous man.

clue.text: A feature of shite channels is electronic wizardry and such

indicators.note: a feature of something is a part of it, so the letters sit inside the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across s-hite and ch-annels

explanation.surface: Rubbish TV stations make up for weak content with flashy gadgetry and effects.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shite' is crude British slang for rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: Hi-tech covers advanced technology such as electronic gadgetry, the sort of wizardry the definition describes.

clue.text: see 12ac.
Ambassador is in Barking, my arse!

indicators.note: barking means mad, so the letters are scrambled into a new order
one piece placed in another goes inside its letters

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs at the idea of a diplomat living in Barking, a working-class east London suburb.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking reads as the London place name; it is the madness that scrambles the letters. 'My arse!' is a British exclamation of disbelief.
explanation.definitionFit: An emissary is an envoy sent on a mission, as an ambassador is sent to represent a state.

clue.text: Castro keen to contain coup

indicators.note: what the words contain is inside them, a run of letters spanning the two

blocks.note: the letters run across ca-stro and ke-en

explanation.surface: The Cuban leader is eager to put down an attempted overthrow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coup' looks like a political putsch in a Cuban setting; the definition is the other sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A coup can be a brilliant success, as in a stroke of genius or a masterstroke.
